qs.q: What is the expected rate of progression to coma and death in children with herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) encephalitis if antiviral therapy is not administered?
qs.e: HSV-1 is a major cause of severe sporadic encephalitis that leads to coma and death in 70% of cases without antiviral treatment. Lower figures underestimate the mortality associated with untreated HSV-1 infection.

qs.q: In cases of Herpes simplex virus encephalitis, which region of the brain is classically and severely affected?
qs.e: In HSV encephalitis, the cerebral cortex, classically the temporal lobes in HSV-1 encephalitis, is often severely affected. Conversely, rabies has a predilection for the basal structures.

qs.q: Which medication is standard first-line therapy for esophageal ulcers associated with herpes simplex virus in HIV patients?
qs.e: Acyclovir is used to treat esophageal ulcers associated with HSV, with doses such as 400mg q5d for 14-21 days. Foscarnet is reserved for unresponsive cases.

qs.q: Which medication is commonly used to treat esophageal ulcers associated with herpes simplex virus in HIV patients?
o: Acyclovir administered orally for mucosal ulcerations
Fluconazole administered orally for fungal lesions
Nitazoxanide administered orally for parasitic infections
Azithromycin administered orally for bacterial pathogens
qs.e: Esophageal ulcers associated with HSV are treated with acyclovir for 14 to 21 days, with foscarnet reserved for unresponsive cases. Fluconazole is used for fungal infections instead.

qs.q: A young adult presents with targetoid skin lesions featuring a pale vesicular center, following a recent herpes simplex virus infection. Which cells are primarily responsible for the direct tissue damage seen in this disorder?
o: Skin-homing cytotoxic T cells attacking basal cells of the skin and mucosae
Neutrophils accumulating beneath the stratum corneum to form subcorneal pustules
CD4+ memory T cells releasing cytokines that induce intercellular epidermal oedema
Mast cells releasing histamine and causing superficial dermal microvascular hyperpermeability
qs.e: Erythema multiforme is driven by skin-homing cytotoxic T cells that attack basal cells displaying cross-reacting antigens. Neutrophil accumulation beneath the stratum corneum is characteristic of impetigo.

qs.q: Which laboratory test finding from a Tzanck smear of a vesicular skin lesion is characteristic of both Herpes Simplex Virus and Varicella-Zoster Virus infections?
o: Multinucleated giant cells with inclusion bodies
Atypical Downey cells with indented nuclei
qs.e: Both HSV and VZV produce multinucleated giant cells and 'ground glass' chromatin on a Tzanck smear. Owl's eye intranuclear inclusions are characteristic of cytomegalovirus histology.

qs.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of acyclovir in the management of Herpes Simplex Virus and Varicella-Zoster Virus infections?
qs.e: Acyclovir acts by inhibiting viral DNA polymerase, thereby halting viral replication during active infection. It does not eliminate viral latency or prevent retrograde transport to ganglia.

qs.q: Which specific antiviral medication is used to treat herpes simplex virus‑related acute liver failure?
qs.e: Acyclovir is the targeted therapy for HSV infection. The other drugs treat different etiologies.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Herpes simplex viruses (HSV‑1, HSV‑2) are DNA viruses that cause mucocutaneous lesions, neonatal disease and encephalitis. They establish latency in sensory ganglia and reactivate under stress or immunosuppression.

sections.p: HSV are enveloped, double‑stranded DNA viruses of the Herpesviridae family. They infect epithelial cells, then travel retrograde to sensory ganglia where they persist as latent genomes.
b: Two main types: HSV‑1 (oral/ocular, also genital) and HSV‑2 (genital, neonatal).
Latency in trigeminal (HSV‑1) or sacral (HSV‑2) ganglia.

sections.p: The virion contains a capsid, tegument and glycoprotein‑rich envelope that mediates entry via heparan sulfate receptors.
b: Enveloped DNA virus; sensitive to drying, heat, detergents.
Glycoproteins gD, gB, gC essential for attachment and fusion.

sections.p: HSV spreads by direct contact with infected secretions or lesions. After replication in epithelium, virions travel to sensory neurons, establish latency, and reactivate when immunity wanes.
b: Oral contact → HSV‑1; sexual contact → HSV‑2.
Neonatal infection via birth canal (HSV‑2) or post‑natal contact (HSV‑1).

sections.p: Clinical manifestations range from mild mucocutaneous vesicles to severe encephalitis and disseminated neonatal disease.
b: Primary oral herpes: painful vesicles → ulceration on lips/face (HSV‑1).
Genital herpes: grouped vesicles → shallow ulcers (HSV‑2, occasional HSV‑1).
Herpes encephalitis: fever, headache, focal deficits, seizures (HSV‑1).
Neonatal HSV: skin, eye, mouth disease; disseminated organ involvement; high mortality without therapy.

sections.p: Laboratory confirmation relies on direct detection of virus or its DNA, especially when clinical picture is atypical.

t.b: Does the lesion contain multinucleated giant cells? Positive result supports HSV but cannot differentiate HSV‑1 vs HSV‑2.

t.a: PCR from lesion swab or CSF
t.b: Is HSV DNA present? Positive result confirms infection; quantitative PCR helps monitor viral load in encephalitis.
Can live virus be grown? Useful where PCR unavailable; slower and less sensitive.
Has the patient seroconverted? IgM indicates recent infection; IgG indicates past exposure, helpful in neonates.

sections.p: Antiviral therapy targets viral DNA polymerase; early treatment reduces morbidity and mortality.
b: Acyclovir (IV for encephalitis, oral for mucocutaneous disease) – selective toxicity via viral thymidine kinase.
Valacyclovir and famciclovir – oral prodrugs with better bioavailability.
Suppressive therapy (daily acyclovir/valacyclovir) for frequent recurrences or HIV co‑infection.

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and clinical practice.
b: HSV‑1 is the leading cause of sporadic encephalitis; treat empirically with IV acyclovir before PCR result.
Neonatal HSV presents as skin‑eye‑mouth disease, disseminated disease, or CNS disease – all need IV acyclovir.
Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells but cannot type HSV; confirm with PCR.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly spreading facial or genital lesions with fever
New onset seizures, altered mental status, or focal neurologic deficits (possible encephalitis)
Neonatal vesicular rash, lethargy, or organ dysfunction

faq.a: No; antivirals suppress replication, but the virus remains latent for life.

faq.q: Why is HSV‑1 more common in encephalitis than HSV‑2?
faq.a: HSV‑1 preferentially travels to the temporal lobe via trigeminal pathways, causing encephalitis.

faq.q: Is a negative Tzanck smear enough to rule out HSV?
faq.a: No; sensitivity is low. PCR is preferred when suspicion remains.
